citation: Hart AM, Wilson ADH, Montovani C, Smith C, Johnson M, Terenghi G, Youle M. Acetyl-l-carnitine: a pathogenesis based treatment for HIV-associated antiretroviral toxic neuropathy. AIDS 2004;18(11):1549–1560
text_quality: ok: publisher PDF with a text layer, 12 pages, complete (figures 1–3, tables 1–3, references). Some symbols are garbled in extraction ('=' as '¼', '<' as ',', '×' as '3', 'Aδ' as 'A'). Page numbers here are PDF pages (PDF 1–12 = journal pages 1549–1560).
design: Prospective open (observational) single-arm cohort with no control group and no randomisation; biopsies of five HIV-negative non-neuropathic volunteers serve as a reference range. Blinded staining and quantification. Analysis by generalized estimating equations on log immunostaining area, adjusted for CD4, age, clinical grade and antiretroviral history; 'intent-to-treat'.
population: 21 HIV-positive adults (age 20–60 at selection; median 40, range 29–60) with established antiretroviral toxic neuropathy (NRTI-associated distal symmetrical polyneuropathy), diagnosed by a neurologist, stable for 2 months, no other neuropathic cause; baseline clinical grade 1 in 8, grade 2 in 10, grade 3 in 3; median neuropathy duration 11 months (2–41). Treatment started March 1999 to October 2001.
n: 21 treated (no comparator arm); 5 HIV-negative reference controls. Biopsies assessed: 16 at 6 months, 6 at 12, 9 at 18, 3 at 24. Two patients died during follow-up.
setting: Royal Free Centre for HIV Medicine and Blond McIndoe Centre, Royal Free and University College Medical School, London, with Blond McIndoe Research Laboratories, University of Manchester, UK.
intervention: Oral acetyl-L-carnitine (ALCAR) 1,500 mg twice daily (3,000 mg/day), 500 mg tablets from Sigma-Tau, for up to 33 months (median follow-up 14 months).
comparator: None (before/after within patients; HIV-negative controls give a reference range only).
duration: Up to 33 months; median follow-up 14 months (range 5–33).
outcomes: Leg skin excision biopsies (an ellipse, lower third of the more symptomatic leg) before treatment and at 6–12-month intervals, up to four per patient. Outcome: immunostaining area fraction (not fibre counts) for PGP 9.5 (all fibres), CGRP (small sensory C and A-delta fibres) and VIP (sympathetic sudomotor fibres) in epidermis, dermis and sweat glands. Clinical 'grade of neuropathic pain' 0–4 defined by analgesic requirement (0 asymptomatic, 1 no analgesia needed, 2 non-opioid analgesics, 3 opioids, 4 pain uncontrolled by opioids). No pain score, VAS, QST or nerve conduction. CD4, CD8, viral load.

key_results.quote: Highly significant increases occurred in both epidermal (mean 100%; P = 0.006) and dermal (mean 133%; P < 0.0001) innervation after 6 months of ALCAR treatment
Patients assessed: 16 at 6 months; 6 at 12 months; 9 at 18 months; 3 at 24 months.
Clinical grade of neuropathic pain improved in 15 of 21 patients overall
The neuropathic grade of five patients was unaffected by treatment, and one patient progressed from grade 1 to 2.
Neuropathic grade improved in 76% of patients and remained unchanged in 19%.
Although not formally documented, those who stopped ALCAR treatment suffered rapid symptom worsening, including return of dysaesthesiae.
ALCAR treatment was well tolerated with no side effects, no adverse events or wound complications.
Compared with HIV-negative controls, total epidermal and dermal innervation reached normal range within 6 months of commencing ALCAR treatment and thereafter remained supranormal
Although epidermal innervation also increased (c) it remained less than that found in normal controls (a).
After the baseline biopsy, 11 patients had one further biopsy, 10 had two and 1 had three.

an observational cohort of 21 patients with established ATN (grade 0–4/4 by analgesic requirement, where 0 is asymptomatic, 1 is ATN but no analgesia required, 2 is ATN requiring non-opioid analgesics, 3 is opioid analgesics required, and 4 is pain uncontrolled by opioid analgesia)

author_limitations.quote: However, a randomized controlled trial utilizing a validated visual analogue pain scale is required to demonstrate conclusive symptomatic benefits.

While there was no placebo arm to this study, the natural history of untreated DSP suggests that the continuous and long-term beneficial effects found in this patient cohort resulted from ALCAR treatment.

The increased ratio of CGRP and VIP to PGP immunostaining found after ALCAR treatment suggests that regenerating fibres may be functional, although electrophysiological and sensory testing will be required for confirmation.
Data from a full randomized controlled trial is now awaited to validate the results of this study and to determine the required duration and dose of ALCAR treatment.

funding_conflicts: Sponsorship: unrestricted grant for laboratory materials from Bristol-Myers-Squibb Pharmaceuticals (UK). Acknowledgements thank staff of Bristol-Myers Squibb and Menotti Calvani of Sigma-tau Farmaceutiche Italia, the ALCAR manufacturer; tablets were Sigma-Tau's. No conflict-of-interest statement printed. Not noted by the authors: the abstract's 76%/19% does not match the results' counts (15, 5 and 1 of 21 = 71%, 24%, 5%); biopsy counts after baseline sum to 22 patients against a cohort of 21; Fig. 1 says epidermal innervation stayed below controls while the results text says it reached the normal range; the abstract gives dermal P < 0.05 where the results give P < 0.0001.
